records.table: Château du Tariquet VSOP is a Bas-Armagnac from one family estate near Eauze, distilled once on its own wood-fired stills from Ugni Blanc and Baco. Expect ripe fruit, flowers and a cool minty edge over oak spice, good neat or as the brandy in a Sidecar.
records.story: The estate takes its name from a seventeenth-century lord, the Sieur du Tariquet, and the house dates armagnac there to 1683 by its own account. In 1912 a bear tamer from Ercé, in the Ariège, and his son pooled their savings to buy it, with about seven hectares of vines, and set about restoring it. A daughter of the family grew up on the estate and married the son of a neighbouring farmer, and through that marriage the estate passed to the Grassa family. In 1985 the estate set up a still of its own, made at Condom in the Armagnac tradition and fired with wood; a second, from the same maker, followed in 2016. Each grape variety is made into wine and distilled apart, and the casks are only lightly toasted, so the fruit of the grape leads the oak. For a bartender the VSOP is the plain lesson that armagnac is a grower's spirit: one estate's vines, one family's stills, and a blend young enough to pour.

records.table: Janneau VSOP is the house blend from Condom, made of eaux-de-vie distilled both ways the appellation allows, once in the continuous Armagnac still and twice in pot stills. Fig, honey and toasted raisins with a little leather, it is a gentle first armagnac neat or in a Sidecar.
records.story: Janneau dates itself to 1851, when its founder set up in the armagnac trade at Condom, in the Gers, and the cellars built that year have served the house for its ageing ever since. Four generations of the family ran the business before it passed, in the 1970s, to the Cognac house Martell. The house's place in the region's history is its stills. Double distillation in pot stills had been barred in Armagnac from 1903, and by the house's account it was allowed back in 1972 at Janneau's request. Since then Janneau has distilled both ways: once through the continuous Armagnac still, whose spirit it says brings intensity and depth, and twice in Charentais pot stills, whose spirit it says brings finesse and precision. Then it blends the two. That is why the Cask Atlas names Janneau when it warns that not every armagnac is distilled once. For a bartender the VSOP is the house's everyday blend at 40 per cent and the bottle that puts both stills in one glass, a fair first pour for a guest who knows Cognac.

records.story: The château at Sorbets, in the heart of the Bas-Armagnac, was built in 1870. In 1974 the Lesgourgues family bought the property, and three generations of the family have run it since. Laubade is a grower's house in the full sense: it distils only the grapes of its own vineyard, and it grows all four of the varieties a bartender meets on armagnac labels, Baco, Ugni Blanc, Folle Blanche and Colombard. Each variety is made into wine and distilled apart in the continuous Armagnac way, and each eau-de-vie is aged on its own before the cellar blends them. The house also coopers its own casks from the oak of Gascon forests, the wood dried in the open air for three years before the barrels are made. Beside its blends it keeps eaux-de-vie of many harvests and releases them as single vintages. For a bartender the VSOP shows what one estate's four grapes give in a single blend, and it is the bottle that makes the four grape names worth learning.

records.story: The house tells its story from 1893, when the founder worked as a travelling distiller, carrying his still from farm to farm across Gascony. He married into the Duffau family, whose vines came into the business, and the family has sold its armagnac under two names ever since, Delord and Marie Duffau, each the name of a forebear, as the importer tells it. His sons set up the house as Delord Frères at Lannepax, and the importer dates the company's official founding to 1925. The brothers sold their Bas-Armagnacs beyond Gascony, as far as the United States, and the family's cellars hold armagnacs going back to 1904. A grandson took over the house in 1963 and was joined by his brother in 1973, and a fourth generation followed. Delord distils both ways the appellation allows: on continuous Armagnac stills, one a Sier built in 1900, for its old armagnacs, and on double-distillation stills for fruitier young spirit. For a bartender the Napoléon teaches two things at once: that one family can sell under two names, and what Napoléon promises on an armagnac label.

records.table: Darroze Les Grands Assemblages 20 Ans is a Bas-Armagnac blended at Roquefort from casks the house has chosen and aged from many growers, none under twenty years in oak. Raisin, fig and caramel over soft, fine tannin: pour it neat, at room temperature.
records.story: The Darroze family kept a restaurant at Villeneuve-de-Marsan, in the Landes, where armagnac was served straight from the barrel. From the late 1960s the son of the house went out into the Bas-Armagnac to choose casks from growers and bottle what he found, and in 1974 he founded the house, by its own account with three casks of estate armagnac from the restaurant's cellar. His idea was that armagnac could be kept like wine: one estate, one harvest, no blending, each bottle naming its grower. That became the house's range of single-estate vintages. The house built its cellars at Roquefort in 1985, and his son joined him in 1994. Les Grands Assemblages is the other half of the work: blends by age, from eight years to sixty, made from many terroirs and harvests so that each keeps one style from year to year, the age on the label held by every part of the blend. For a bartender the 20 Ans teaches what an armagnac éleveur does: chooses, ages and blends casks from other people's vines.
